# The Problem

R already has conventions and tooling for code style. [lintr](https://lintr.r-lib.org/) [@hester2025], [air](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/) and [jarl](https://jarl.etiennebacher.com/) are widely used, and it's normal for a package to enforce them on CI, but there's nothing similar for documentation.
`R CMD check` confirms that documentation exists and matches the function signatures, but whether a human can actually read it is left to authors and reviewers.
That applies to the help pages, vignettes and READMEs users see as much as to the comments contributors rely on.

Documentation that's hard to read, whether because of long dense sentences or a tone that assumes things are obvious, increases cognitive load [@sweller1988], frustrates users, and puts people off using a package at all.
rOpenSci's [software review process](https://devguide.ropensci.org/) asks reviewers to judge whether documentation is clear and sufficient, but reviewers are doing that by hand.
More packages are also being written with the help of, or entirely by, AI tools, and without something checking, the result is often verbose.

There's been some prior work, including my own. The [docreview](https://github.com/thisisnic/docreview) package was on CRAN from 2021 to 2024 with five checks including readability scores, and stalled because its architecture was more complicated than it needed to be. The [spelling](https://docs.ropensci.org/spelling/) package checks words but not prose.
Outside R, [Vale](https://vale.sh) is a mature prose linter with packaged style guides that runs in editors and on CI. It handles Markdown and can extract comment text from R files, but it knows nothing about how an R package is laid out or what R vocabulary looks like, and you have to install and configure a separate binary to use it.

What's missing is an opinionated documentation linter for R packages that's usable from R and helps both humans and AI tools write better docs.
